title: The Necklace
focus: the cost of wanting to seem richer than you are

teacherSummary.text: Mathilde Loisel, a clerk's wife who dreams of luxury, borrows a diamond necklace from her rich friend Madame Forestier for a ministry ball. She loses it, and the Loisels secretly buy a replacement for 36,000 francs, sinking into poverty for ten years to repay the debt. Worn and aged, Mathilde meets Madame Forestier and tells her the truth. The original was paste, worth at most five hundred francs.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this story is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “The Necklace,” how does Maupassant show the cost of wanting to seem richer than you are? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the irony you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In The Necklace, how does Maupassant develop the idea of the cost of wanting to seem richer than you are? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the irony in the story helps build that idea. Read in the public-domain translation by Jonathan Sturges.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how The Necklace develops the idea of the cost of wanting to seem richer than you are. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of irony and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim. Read in the public-domain translation by Jonathan Sturges.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of The Necklace (where it begins, turns and ends) and its irony shape the reader's understanding of the cost of wanting to seem richer than you are. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning. Distinguish what is directly stated from what is really meant.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what The Necklace suggests about the cost of wanting to seem richer than you are. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the story's irony and characterization), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay. Distinguish what is directly stated from what is really meant.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Guy de Maupassant uses irony in The Necklace to complicate the reader's understanding of the cost of wanting to seem richer than you are. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate The Necklace within its historical and literary context and argue how the story's treatment of the cost of wanting to seem richer than you are responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read The Necklace alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the story's handling of the cost of wanting to seem richer than you are follows or bends those conventions, using the irony as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to The Necklace and its treatment of the cost of wanting to seem richer than you are. State your method, show what it reveals in the story's irony and characterization, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads The Necklace as evidence for a larger claim about the cost of wanting to seem richer than you are in The Necklace. Connect close reading of the story to the whole story, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads The Necklace as a hinge in the story's larger treatment of the cost of wanting to seem richer than you are. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on The Necklace.

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Why do people sometimes pretend to be more than they are? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board. Before we start, a content note: Nothing in this story needs a special warning.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are bracelets, vestibule, contrasted, humiliating, homeward. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check the definition. Here is the first: “She saw first of all some bracelets, then a pearl necklace, then a Venetian cross, gold, and precious stones of admirable workmanship.” In this sentence it means: bands or chains worn around the wrist. Word histories: For the other words, look up the word history (Etymonline or the OED) and record the language of origin and the root meaning in your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of The Necklace would have known. Published in Le Gaulois in 1884. Translation: Jonathan Sturges, in The Odd Number (1889), public domain in the US. Why does this story matter? One of the best-known twist endings; on Glencoe grade 9 lesson plans. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for irony.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. The passage opens: “She saw first of all some bracelets, then a pearl necklace, then a Venetian cross, gold, and precious stones of admirable workmanship.” I stop and ask: what is the author doing here, and how does it connect to the cost of wanting to seem richer than you are? I circle “bracelets”, one of today's words, and ask why the author chose it over a plainer word. When I find irony, I underline it and write its effect in the margin, then I check my idea against the next sentence.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for irony.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of irony. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.

segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Irony, Characterization, Theme: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; the app shows the level your teacher assigned (for a 9–10 class, the HS Sophomore prompt reads: Analyze how The Necklace develops the idea of the cost of wanting to seem richer than you are. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of irony and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim. Read in the public-domain translation by Jonathan Sturges.) I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion from the 30 tiered questions (focus set for the class level): wait time, think-pair-share on DOK 3/4, follow-up probes.
segments.script: Let's talk. We move from what happens to why it matters to whether it's right. After each question I wait before calling on anyone: think first. Our anchor question: How does this story connect to vanity and appearance? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence, and end by writing one question of your own.

segments.activity: Story quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the story quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this story suggests about the cost of wanting to seem richer than you are, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how irony shapes the cost of wanting to seem richer than you are. Tonight, read the next story and add two words to your etymology log.

routine: Bell-ringer: post one literal and one evaluative question; students jot before talking (wait time).
Discussion (10 min): run the focus questions for the class level in order, literal to evaluative; think-pair-share every DOK 3/4 item.
After each answer, use a follow-up probe before moving on; ask a second student to agree, extend or challenge.
Exit: each student writes one question of their own (student-generated) for tomorrow’s opener.
